           DIRECT TESTIMONY AND EXHIBITS OF ANTHONY M. GEORGIS

 1                   I.       INTRODUCTION AND QUALIFICATIONS

 2   Q1.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME, POSITION, AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.    My name is Anthony M. Georgis. I am the Managing Director of the Energy Practice

 4         at NewGen Strategies and Solutions, LLC (“NewGen”). My business address is 225

 5         Union Boulevard, Suite 450, Lakewood, Colorado 80228. NewGen is a consulting firm

 6         that specializes in utility rates, engineering economics, financial accounting, asset

 7         valuation, appraisals, and business strategy for electric, natural gas, water, wastewater,

 8         and solid waste utilities.

 9   Q2.   PLEASE OUTLINE YOUR FORMAL EDUCATION.

10   A.    I have a Master of Business Administration from Texas A&M University with a

11         specialization in finance. I also earned a Bachelor of Science in Mechanical

12         Engineering from Texas A&M University. In addition to my undergraduate and

13         graduate degrees, I am a registered Professional Engineer in the state of Colorado.

14   Q3.   PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE.

15   A.    I am the Managing Director of NewGen’s Energy Practice. I have more than 25 years

16         of experience in engineering and economic analyses for the energy, water, and waste

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-07507                  1                  Direct Testimony & Exhibits
     PUC Docket No. 58796                                                  of Anthony M. Georgis
  1         resources industries. My work includes various assignments for private industry, local

 2         governments, and utilities, including sustainability strategy, strategic planning,

 3         financial and economic analyses, cost of service (“COS”) and rate studies, energy

 4         efficiency, and market research. I have been extensively involved in the development

 5         of unbundled COS and pricing models during my career. A summary of my

 6         qualifications is provided within Exhibit AMG-1 to this testimony.

 7   Q4.   HAVE YOU TESTIFIED BEFORE ANY REGULATORY COMMISSIONS?

 8   A.    Yes. I have submitted testimony to the Florida Public Service Commission, the Public

 9         Utility Commission of Texas (“PUCT”), the California Public Utilities Commission,

10         the Arizona Corporation Commission, and the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission,

11         as shown in my resume and record of testimony included as Exhibit AMG-1.

12   Q5.   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU SUBMITTING THIS TESTIMONY?

13   A.    I am testifying on behalf of the Cities Advocating Reasonable Deregulation (“CARD”).

14   Q6.   WAS YOUR TESTIMONY PREPARED BY YOU OR UNDER YOUR DIRECT

15         SUPERVISION?

16   A.    Yes, it was.

17                          II.      PURPOSE OF TESTIMONY

18   Q7.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

19   A.    The purpose of my testimony is to present my review, analysis, and recommendations

20         regarding the Southwestern Electric Power Company’s (“SWEPCO” or “Company”)

21         proposed Standard Form Contract for Electric Service – Large Loads (“ES-LL”).

22         SWEPCO states that its current Contract for Electric Service is not designed for large


     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-07507                2                  Direct Testimony & Exhibits
     PUC Docket No. 58796                                                of Anthony M. Georgis
  1            loads such as data centers that are anticipated to come online in its service territory in

 2            the near future and that it must update its contract to meet the new risks related to these

 3            customers. 1

 4   Q8.      PLEASE DESCRIBE SWEPCO’S APPROACH TO ADDRESSING THE

 5            UNPRECEDENTED EXPECTED GROWTH IN LARGE LOAD AND DATA

 6            CENTERS.

 7   A.       SWEPCO states that its current Contract for Electric Service is not designed for the

 8            large loads that the Company is expecting to come online in the near future. 2 As the

 9            projected individual large loads are likely to be 500 megawatts (“MW”) to 1,000 MW

10            or more each, equaling approximately 10% to 20% of SWEPCO’s total system peak

11            demand, the increased risk and concerns related to these individual loads and customers

12            necessitate a new ES-LL. SWEPCO notes that a single data center or large load

13            customer could eclipse the entire residential sector for the Company in Texas. 3

14   Q9.      WHAT ARE SOME OF THE MOST SIGNIFICANT RISKS UTILITIES FACE

15            WHEN PROVIDING SERVICE TO THESE NEW LARGE LOAD AND DATA

16            CENTERS?

17   A.       As these new data center customers require large amounts of infrastructure and power

18            supply services that may rival entire customer classes for a utility, there is a significant

19            risk related to stranded costs or shifting costs from the new large load to the existing

20            customers on the system. If SWEPCO, or any utility, does not have a standard approach

 2            risk of shifting costs from the new large load to the existing customers and customer

 3            classes.

 4   Q10. PLEASE DESCRIBE THE GENERAL APPLICABILITY AND TERMS OF

 5            THE PROPOSED ES-LL.

 6   A.       The ES-LL includes several elements, terms, and conditions of service in an attempt to

 7            ensure the recovery of the costs to serve large loads. Some of the critical elements in

 8            the ES-LL include:

 9            •     Application to any single facility, or for multiple facilities in aggregate, whose

10                  capacity needs or customer demand is greater than or equal to 75 MW.

11            •     Definition of the Ramp Period as “the period between the beginning initial date of

12                  service to a new large load customer and the day before the first day on which the

13                  customer takes service at its full Contract Capacity.” 4

14            •     Definition of the Full Operations Period as “the period beginning on the large load

15                  customer’s expected first day taking service at the full contracted capacity through

16                  the end of the customer’s Initial Contract Term and any Renewal Term.” 5

17            •     Application of a minimum bill in both the Ramp and Full Operations periods. This

18                  includes minimum billing demand and energy amounts tied to the customer’s

19                  contracted capacity. This attempts to ensure that SWEPCO recovers fixed

     5

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-07507                      4                  Direct Testimony & Exhibits
     PUC Docket No. 58796                                                      of Anthony M. Georgis
  1                  infrastructure costs even if actual customer usage falls below the contracted

 2                  amounts.

3             •     The 12-year initial term auto-renews for 1-year periods annually with a 5-year exit

4                   notice requirement. 6

5             •     Early termination triggers a fee equal to all remaining minimum payments. 7

 6            •     Financial collateral requirements equivalent to 24 months of non-fuel bills. 8


 7   Q11. DOES THE 12-YEAR TERM OF THE CONTRACT START AT THE

 8            BEGINNING OF SERVICE OR WHEN THE CUSTOMER REACHES ITS

 9            FULL OPERATIONS PERIOD?

10   A.       The 12-year term of the contract begins once the customer reaches the Full Operations

11            Period, which starts the first day that the customer reaches its full contracted capacity.

12            This 12-year term is likely to start 2 to 4 years after the customer initially receives

13            service. Thus, the full initial term of the contract will likely be 14 to 16 years inclusive

14            of the Ramp and Full Operations periods.

15                           III.   SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATIONS

16   Q12. WHAT KEY ISSUES OR CONCERNS DID YOU IDENTIFY IN THE

17            PROPOSED ES-LL?

18   A.       I identified two key concerns regarding the proposed ES-LL terms and conditions that

19            each pose a risk and contribute to potential stranded costs that may be borne by existing


     6
          Id. at 21:15–19.
     7
          Id. at 22:9–21.
     8
          Id. at 23:10–11.

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-07507                      5                  Direct Testimony & Exhibits
     PUC Docket No. 58796                                                      of Anthony M. Georgis
 1             customers. These include:

 2            1.    The contract term length of 12 years after the customer reaches the Full Operations

 3                  Period 9 is too short and is not aligned with power supply or generation asset costs

4                   and useful lives likely procured and incurred on behalf of large loads.

5             2.    The minimum demand and energy determinants should be publicly stated for each

6                   contract and should be consistent with a minimum of 90% of contracted demand

7                   and energy amounts.

 8   Q13. FURTHER DESCRIBE THE ISSUES WITH THE CONTRACT TERM OF 12

 9            YEARS.

10   A.       SWEPCO, or any utility serving data centers and large loads of this magnitude, is likely

11            to incur long-term cost obligations or need to construct generation assets with useful

12            lives of 35 years or longer. Natural gas combined cycle generation plants are a common

13            technology deployed and constructed for serving large loads with high load factors such

14            as data centers. These generation plants often have a useful life of 35 years or more if

15            they are maintained. Thus, utilities recover the costs associated with those assets over

16            that same useful life period: 35 years or more, not the 12 years identified in the ES-LL.

17            SWEPCO’s parent company AEP even documents the useful life of its natural gas

18            combined cycle generation plants as 35 years. 10




     9
          Id. at 20: 5–6.
     10

          Direct Testimony of Witness David Davis, Executive Summary of David A. Davis at 3 and Exhibit DAD-1
          (Aug. 28, 2009).

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-07507                       6                    Direct Testimony & Exhibits
     PUC Docket No. 58796                                                         of Anthony M. Georgis
  1              As the Company may commit to costs of up to 35 years or more, 11 it is critical to apply

 2              cost recovery terms and conditions in the ES-LL that align with that long-term

 3              commitment. If the contract term or length is not aligned with the useful lives of the

 4              assets procured for the customer, it may lead to stranded costs and cost shifting to

 5              existing customers who were not responsible for the incremental infrastructure or

 6              generation and transmission costs. SWEPCO’s 12-year term after the first day of Full

 7              Operations Period attempts to address these stranded costs that may arise from the

 8              Company serving these customers. However, SWEPCO’s 12-year term may not be

 9              aligned with the useful life of the assets or the length of time during which the Company

10              is committing to incur costs.

11   Q14. DOES SWEPCO STATE THAT THE RESOURCES AND COSTS INCURRED

12              TO PROVIDE SERVICE TO THE LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS MATCH THE

13              12-YEAR TERM OF THE CONTRACT?

14   A.         No. In fact, the Company admits that “SWEPCO must secure resources years ahead to

15              meet customer demand. Long-term investments often exceed 12 years, and industry

16              practice includes contracts longer than 12 years.” 12 SWEPCO goes on to state that

17              “Ultimately, a longer contract better protects all customers from additional capacity

18              costs if a large load customer leaves the system.” 13 Based on these statements, it

19              appears that SWEPCO is fully aware of the situation and is admitting that it will incur

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-07507                         7                  Direct Testimony & Exhibits
     PUC Docket No. 58796                                                         of Anthony M. Georgis
  1            or commit to costs and assets with useful lives of more than 12 years to serve large

 2            loads and data centers.

 3   Q15. WHAT HAPPENS WHEN SWEPCO INCURS OR COMMITS TO COSTS

 4            WITH USEFUL LIVES OR COST RECOVERY PERIODS THAT ARE

 5            GREATER THAN THE 12-YEAR CONTRACT TERM?

 6   A.       If SWEPCO incurs costs related to an asset that has a useful life of more than 12 years,

 7            the Company runs the risk of not fully recovering the costs over the life of the ES-LL.

 8            This would lead to remaining or stranded costs putting the remaining customers on

 9            SWEPCO’s system at risk for paying for the stranded costs.

10   Q16. CAN YOU PROVIDE AN ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE OF THE RISK OF

11            STRANDED COSTS?

12   A.       Yes. Given that the useful lives of the assets or costs incurred to provide large load

13            service are up to 35 years or more in length, a 12-year contact term would result in

14            SWEPCO recovering approximately 34% of the total costs of these assets, leaving up

15            to 66% of the remaining costs to be recovered from other customers. To further put that

16            commitment in perspective to SWEPCO’s current costs, as previously mentioned, the

17            load of just one of these data center customers could rival the entire load of the existing

18            residential customer class currently served by SWEPCO. That means that the risk of

19            stranded costs for just one of these data center customers could rival the full annual

20            generation revenue requirement for the residential class and that the stranded costs

21            could be applied for up to 23 or more years after the termination date of the ES-LL. 14



     14
          35-year useful life of a generation plant less 12 years of required contract recovery leaves up to 23 years of
          cost recovery remaining.

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-07507                            8                      Direct Testimony & Exhibits
     PUC Docket No. 58796                                                                of Anthony M. Georgis
  1   Q17. WHAT IS THE IMPACT OR RESULT OF THESE RISKS FOR EXISTING

 2            CUSTOMERS ON SWEPCO’S SYSTEM?

 3   A.       If these potential stranded costs are not accounted for or recovered from the large load

 4            or data center customers over their contracted term, SWEPCO would likely seek to

 5            shift cost recovery to the existing customers in SWEPCO’s system. These potential

 6            stranded costs could become enormous in the face of SWEPCO’s statement on growth.

 7            As an example, if 1,000 MW of expected load and required generation assets become

8             stranded at the end of the initial 12-year contract term, it could lead to about $78 million

9             per year of stranded costs or additional costs that existing customers would have to

10            pay. 15 Please note that this estimate is conservative and only includes annual

11            depreciation and return and no annual operating and maintenance expenses, which

12            would also be incurred.

13   Q18. WHY DOES SWEPCO PROPOSE A 12-YEAR TERM WHEN IT ADMITS

14            THAT IT IS LIKELY TO INCUR COSTS OR ASSETS WITH USEFUL LIVES

15            THAT EXCEED 12 YEARS?

16   A.       SWEPCO states that the “contract term of twelve years provides a reasonable assurance

17            that these customers will take service over a period long enough to provide a substantial

18            contribution to the cost of these investments and financial commitments.” 16 Based on

19            this statement, SWEPCO must believe that as long as the customer provides a

20            “substantial contribution to the costs,” the term of the ES-LL is reasonable.



     15
          1,000 MW at $1,000 per kW construction amortized over 35 years results in annual depreciation expenses of
          $28 million per year plus 9% rate of return on the marginal new rate base for the plant starting at the net plant
          value in year 13 (~$50 million per year) for a total of $78 million.
     16
          Docket No. 58796, Direct Testimony of Melissa A. Gage at 20:17–21:1–3.

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-07507                              9                      Direct Testimony & Exhibits
     PUC Docket No. 58796                                                                  of Anthony M. Georgis
  1   Q19. DOES SWEPCO PROVIDE, QUANTIFY, OR DEFINE “SUBSTANTIAL

 2            CONTRIBUTION TO THE COSTS”?

 3   A.       No. SWEPCO does not provide or quantify the percentage of total costs incurred or an

 4            amount that would meet the “substantial contribution” statement. However, that

 5            amount could be as low as 34% of the total costs as noted in my previous illustrative

 6            example of stranded costs.

 7   Q20. IS A “SUBSTANTIAL CONTRIBUTION TO THE COSTS” EQUIVALENT TO

 8            THE FULL COSTS INCURRED BY SWEPCO?

 9   A.       No. By SWEPCO’s own admission, it believes that it will incur costs to serve the

10            customers that will exceed the term of the ES-LL.

11   Q21. HAS THE FEDERAL GOVERNMENT,                                    PUCT, STATE OF TEXAS

12            LEGISLATURE, OR GOVERNOR INTRODUCED ANY RULES OR

13            LEGISLATION REGARDING ELECTRIC UTILITIES RECOVERING THE

14            COSTS TO SERVE DATA CENTERS?

15   A.       Yes. On a national level, leading United States hyperscalers and Artificial Intelligence

16            (“AI”) companies pledged to build, bring, or buy all the energy needed for building and

17            operating data centers as part of President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge. 17

18            In Texas, Senate Bill 6 requires large loads and data centers of 75 MW or more to pay

19            for interconnection studies and infrastructure upgrades, demonstrate financial

20            assurance, and provide emergency curtailment/disconnect obligations. 18 In addition,



     17
          Ratepayer Protection Pledge, White House (Mar. 4, 2026),
          https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/.
     18
          Tex. S.B. 6, 89th Leg., R.S. (2025).

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-07507                         10                    Direct Testimony & Exhibits
     PUC Docket No. 58796                                                            of Anthony M. Georgis
 1               Governor Abbott sent a letter to the PUCT directing the Commission to “take action to

2               require data centers to pay for all of their electric infrastructure costs to ensure that no

3               residential ratepayer is burdened by those costs.” 19 Although the Governor’s letter

4               mentioned data centers that interconnect to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas

5               (“ERCOT”) grid, the letter’s aim was “[t]o guarantee any data center development does

 6              not come at the cost of Texans and our local communities.” 20 Thus, it is reasonable that

 7              the letter’s directives should apply to utilities outside of ERCOT, including SWEPCO.

 8   Q22. DOES SWEPCO’S PROPOSED ES-LL AND 12-YEAR TERM MEET EITHER

 9              THE PRESIDENT’S OR THE GOVERNOR’S DIRECTIVES OF REQUIRING

10              DATA      CENTERS         TO     PAY      FOR      ALL      OF     THEIR       ELECTRIC

11              INFRASTRUCTURE COSTS TO ENSURE THAT NO RESIDENTIAL

12              RATEPAYER IS BURDENED BY THOSE COSTS?

13   A.         No. As previously stated in my testimony, SWEPCO will likely commit to and incur

14              costs that are much longer than the 12-year term or minimum requirement for ES-LL

15              service. If and as large load customers terminate service at the 12-year term of the ES-

16              LL or before the useful life of the infrastructure acquired to serve them, the risk remains

17              that SWEPCO will seek to shift those remaining or stranded costs to other customers,

18              including residential ratepayers.

2          companies have already agreed to do in the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. Such a term

4    Q23. HOW CAN SWEPCO ADDRESS THESE RISKS IN ITS PROPOSED ES-LL?

5    A.    There are multiple ways to mitigate these stranded cost risks; however, I recommend

6          focusing on recovering the full cost of the assets or generation revenue requirements

7          incurred to serve the ES-LL customers from the individual customers responsible for

 8         those costs. I recommend two options:

 9         1.   Recover the full amortized cost of the generation plant or individual generation

10              revenue requirements over the term of the ES-LL, thus changing the number of

11              years associated with the contract, or


12         2.   Require a financial obligation on behalf of the customer (e.g., letter of credit or

13              surety bond) equivalent to the balance of the remaining revenue requirement after

14              the 12-year contract term associated with its generation service (i.e., the stranded

15              asset amount).


16         If SWEPCO aligns the term of the ES-LL with the lives of the assets procured, it could

17         enter into 10- to 15-year Power Purchase Agreements (“PPAs”) for each customer and

18         assign that full cost to them to recover over the 12-year term of the ES-LL, or the

19         Company could increase the term of the ES-LL to 15 years to align with the

20         amortization period and term of the PPA. This would fully align the contract term in

21         years with the full revenue requirement and cost recovery of the asset(s). The second

22         option is similar; however, instead of aligning the term or length of years of the ES-LL


     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-07507                 12                  Direct Testimony & Exhibits
     PUC Docket No. 58796                                                  of Anthony M. Georgis
  1         with the asset life (e.g., 15 years as noted above), SWEPCO could maintain the 12-year

 2         term and require a financial reserve, security, or cash reserve available for the amount

 3         of the stranded costs remaining after the 12-year term of the ES-LL. This second option

 4         may be more desirable if a data center customer is a long-term customer beyond the

 5         initial contract term of 12 years as they would simply continue taking service after the

 6         12 years and draw down the potential stranded costs and financial security amount over

 7         time until they became $0.

8    Q24. WHAT DO YOU RECOMMEND TO ADDRESS THESE ISSUES OF

9          STRANDED COSTS AND COST SHIFTING TO EXISTING CUSTOMERS

10         WHO NEVER DROVE THE RISK OF NOR MATERIALLY BENEFITED

11         FROM THE INVESTMENTS?

12   A.    SWEPCO should adjust or modify its proposed ES-LL language to include a clause or

13         clauses to ensure that the Company fully mitigates the risk of stranded cost shifting to

14         existing customers. This can include either or both of the two options I propose to

15         ensure that the full costs incurred by SWEPCO on behalf of and directly serving the

16         data center and large loads are fully recovered from those customers causing the costs

17         and not existing customers who did not and will not materially benefit from the

18         investments. SWEPCO should modify the proposed ES-LL to include a financial

19         obligation, letter of credit, escrow account, or some other financial security that is

20         equivalent to the quantified stranded costs incurred after the currently proposed 12-year

21         ES-LL term to serve the customers.




     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-07507                 13                 Direct Testimony & Exhibits
     PUC Docket No. 58796                                                 of Anthony M. Georgis
 1    Q25. DO YOU HAVE ANY OTHER RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING THE

2             ES-LL?

3    A.       Yes. I recommend that the minimum demand and energy determinants should be

 4            publicly stated rather than kept confidential and/or redacted for the ES-LL. I

 5            recommend that a consistent minimum of 90% of contracted demand and energy

 6            amounts be used for the ES-LL.

 7   Q26. WHY DO YOU RECOMMEND 90% MINIMUM DEMAND AND ENERGY

 8            DETERMINANTS?

 9   A.       These minimum demand and energy billing determinants are not commonly

10            confidential and are often publicly stated for all potential customers to see. As seen in

11            Witness Gage’s testimony, Table 4 – Minimum Demand Provision Examples from

12            non-AEP Vertically-Integrated Electric Utilities, nine different utilities across the

13            country are publicly stating their minimum demand levels. 21 In addition, several of the

14            example tariffs referenced publicly require a 90% or higher minimum demand or

15            ratchet. Setting the minimum to 90% further ensures direct cost recovery and less risk

16            of stranded costs on an annual and long-term contract term basis. This also ensures that

17            the large load will pay at least 90% of the cost incurred, even if they do not meet their

18            contracted consumption and demand levels used to determine the rates. This further

19            limits any cost shifting to a maximum of 10% of the capital expenditures and operating

20            costs over the life of the ES-LL.

          Docket No. 58796, Direct Testimony of Melissa A. Gage at 19:5–7.

  1   Q27. WHY SHOULD SWEPCO PUBLICLY STATE THE MINIMUM ENERGY

 2         AND DEMAND DETERMINANT AMOUNTS?

 3   A.    By publicly stating the minimum demand and energy determinants for billing,

 4         SWEPCO ensures equity and transparency across the contracts for any customer taking

 5         service under the ES-LL. If varying levels of minimum demand and energy

 6         determinants are set for each ES-LL, it could increase risk, volatility, and potential

 7         stranded costs for SWEPCO that could be imposed on existing customers.

 8   Q28. DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR TESTIMONY?

 9   A.    Yes, it does. However, I reserve the right to incorporate new information that may

10         subsequently become available. I also reserve the right to supplement my testimony if

11         SWEPCO, intervenors, or other parties submit new or corrected information in

12         connection with this proceeding.

       David A. Davis, Principal Accounting Consultant for American Electric Power Service

Corporation, testifies with regard to the depreciation expense for Southwestern Electric Power

Company (SWEPCO).          Based on the depreciation study he performed of SWEPCO's

Texas jurisdictional annual depreciation expense is approximately $46 million as recommended

 SWEPCO's existing depreciation rates would produce.

        The methods and procedures utilized by Mr. Davis are described in the depreciation study

 for SWEPCO attached to his testimony. All of the property was considered on a group plan,

 where depreciation is accrued upon the basis of the original cost of all property included in each

 depreciable plant group. The dollars in each primary plant account are considered as a separate

 group for depreciation accounting purposes and an annual depreciation rate for each account is

 determined. For SWEPCO's study, the plant groups consisted of the individual primary plant

 accounts for Production, Transmission, Distribution, and General Plant property.

        The depreciation rates were calculated by the Average Remaining Life Method. For

 Production Plant, the generating unit retirement dates and the interim retirement history for the

retirement characteristics of the property described using the Iowa-type retirement dispersion

 1    A.   There are two basic methods commonly utilized to calculate depreciation rates. They

2         are the Average Life Method (sometimes referred to as the Whole Life Method) and

3         the Average Remaining Life Method.

4                 The Average Life Method recovers the original cost of the plant, adjusted for

5         net salvage, over the average service life of the investment. The basic assumptions

6         used in determining depreciation rates by the Average Life Method are: 1) property

7         will be retired over a specified average life; and 2) the future amount of net salvage is

 8        known. Neither of these assumptions can be confirmed until the entire property group

9         is retired. The major shortcoming of the Average Life Method is that it does not

10        provide a mechanism to adjust accumulated depreciation when changes occur in

11         service life or net salvage.

12                 The Average Remaining Life Method compensates for this shortfall by

13         recovering the original cost of the plant, adjusted for net salvage, less accumulated

14         depreciation over the average remaining life of the plant.

       DISCUSSION OF METHODS AND PROCEDURES USED IN THE STUDY



1.     Group Method
               All of the depreciable property included in this report was considered on a group

       plan. Under the group plan, depreciation expense is accrued upon the basis of the

       original cost ofall property included in each depreciable plant account. Upon retirement

       ofanypdepreciable property, its full cost, less any net salvage realized, is charged to the

       accrued depreciation reserve regardless of the age of the particular item retired.. Also,

       under this plan, the dollars in each primary plant account are considered a separate group

       for depreciation accounting purposes and an annual depreciation rate for each account is

       determined. The annual accruals by primary account were then summed, to arrive at the

       total accrual for each functional group.. The total accrual divided by the original cost

       yields the functional group accrual rate.



2.     Determination of'Annual Depreciation Rates By the Average Remaining Life Method



        SWEPCO's current depreciation rates are based on the Average Remaining Life Method

       for Production, Transmission, Distribution and General Plant.

        The Average Remaining Life Method recovers the original cost of the plant, adjusted for

       net salvage, less the accumulated depreciation, over the average remaining life of the

        plant. By this method, the annual depreciation rate for each account is determined on the

        each particular survivor

13             customer could eclipse the entire residential sector for the Company in Texas.3

       David A. Davis, Principal Accounting Consultant for American Electric Power Service

Corporation, testifies with regard to the depreciation expense for Southwestern Electric Power

Company (SWEPCO).          Based on the depreciation study he performed of SWEPCO's

Generation, Transmission, Distribution and General Plant depreciable electric utility plant in

Texas jurisdictional annual depreciation expense is approximately $46 million as recommended

 SWEPCO's existing depreciation rates would produce.

        The methods and procedures utilized by Mr. Davis are described in the depreciation study

 for SWEPCO attached to his testimony. All of the property was considered on a group plan,

 where depreciation is accrued upon the basis of the original cost of all property included in each

 depreciable plant group. The dollars in each primary plant account are considered as a separate

 group for depreciation accounting purposes and an annual depreciation rate for each account is

 determined. For SWEPCO's study, the plant groups consisted of the individual primary plant

 accounts for Production, Transmission, Distribution, and General Plant property.

        The depreciation rates were calculated by the Average Remaining Life Method. For

 Production Plant, the generating unit retirement dates and the interim retirement history for the

lives.    The average service lives for Transmission, Distribution, and General Plant were

determined using statistical procedures similar to those used in the insurance industry in studies

of mortality.   The historical retirement experience of the property groups was studied and

retirement characteristics of the property described using the Iowa-type retirement dispersion

curves.    Removal and salvage amounts specific to final removal of SWEPCO's generating

stations at the end of their useful life were based on dismantling studies performed by SWEPCO

companies, such as SWEPCO, continue to collect such costs through depreciation rates
